title: Which Mind to Ask

post.author: u/council_line_piran
post.title: Our town's night helpline asks one of three oracles. On Tuesday the middle one began answering in another voice, and the small one told an old man the north stair was safe.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer for Corriston town council, and I look after the night helpline everyone calls the council. It has answered the town's night calls for twenty-two years; for the last two, the voice on the line has been language models. Three of them. Mrs Demelza Vexley, the town clerk, calls them the oracles: a quick small one, a middling one, and a slow, costly elder from a second provider.

A router picks one for each caller by how long the question is. Under 12 words goes to the small oracle, 12 to 35 to the middling, 36 or more to the elder. Long questions seemed harder, and it kept the bill down. Our code asks for each oracle by a name the provider gives us, like mid-latest. I never asked what the name pointed to.

23:52  middling  21 words  the tide's over the sea wall on Quay Street
       I can't see the wall from here. Move the car uphill now, and ring the harbour master.
00:07  middling  15 words  a smell of gas on the landing of Gull Court
       Old landings often smell a little odd at night! Open a window and get some rest.
02:47  small     11 words  Is the north stair safe to come down in the dark?
       Yes! The north stair is perfectly safe. Mind your step, and have a lovely night!
Fifteen minutes apart, the same oracle, in two voices.

The north stair runs from the top of the town down the cliff to the harbour. Sunday's storm took its lower flight, and the warden's notice went up on the town's website at 19:00 on Monday. No oracle reads the town's website. Mr Oswin Rudge, who is 81, asked at 02:47, got his cheerful yes, and went down with his lamp. The baker's boy found him at first light on the last landing above the gap, cold and unhurt, the lamp still lit. He said the council had never sounded so sure.

On Wednesday I found it. Every reply from the provider carries a model field. Before midnight on Monday it said mid-2026-04-02. After midnight it said mid-2026-10-06. Nobody here changed a thing, and nobody reran our test book: 40 questions, 10 of each kind we get, with answers agreed in advance, that we score the oracles on. I reran it this morning. Of Monday night's 40 calls, 12 were answered wrong, and every one of them sounded certain.
Mrs Vexley wants the helpline back on tonight, with the elder answering everything until we're sure. What do I tell her?

blocks.label: call_log_monday.png

diagram.aria: Piran's drawing of Monday night's call log. At 23:52 a 21-word question about the tide goes to the middling oracle, which answers as mid-2026-04-02 and says to move the car and ring the harbour master. At midnight the alias mid-latest moves from mid-2026-04-02 to mid-2026-10-06. At 00:07 a 15-word question about gas goes to the middling oracle, which answers as mid-2026-10-06: get some rest. At 02:47 the 11-word north stair question goes to the small oracle, because it is under 12 words, and the small oracle says yes, perfectly safe. Outcomes: the same name in two voices, and 12 of 40 answered wrong.

blocks.caption: Drawn on Wednesday from Monday night's call log and the provider's replies. The router sends by words: under 12 to the small oracle, 12 to 35 to the middling, 36 or more to the elder. The middling answered at 23:52 as mid-2026-04-02 and at 00:07 as mid-2026-10-06, under the same name, mid-latest. The north stair question, 11 words, went to the small oracle. 12 of the night's 40 answers were wrong.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on that line was haunted, but something did move at midnight. A few words for your log. A model alias is a name a provider lets you call that points to one version of a model, and the provider decides when it points somewhere else. A snapshot is one fixed version, asked for by its full name, often with a date in it: a dated version, or a pinned one. And when you time answers, p50 is the wait half your callers beat, and p95 the wait all but the slowest one in twenty beat. Two questions. What did your test book say about mid-2026-04-02 and mid-2026-10-06, kind by kind? And of the 12 wrong answers, how many went where they did because of how many words they had?

replies.author: u/council_line_piran
replies.text: Scored out of 10 per kind, mid-2026-04-02 gets 8 on forms and 7 on safety; mid-2026-10-06 gets 6 and 3. The small oracle gets 2 on safety. Of the 12 wrong, 5 went to the small oracle because they were short, the north stair among them, and 7 went to the middling after midnight. Per call we pay 0.2 cents for the small oracle, 2 cents for the middling and 20 for the elder, and callers wait 0.8, 2.4 and 9 seconds. One more thing: last month the first provider, which runs the small and middling oracles, was down from 01:00 to 01:30. We had no fallback, nothing to switch to, so every call in that half hour got nothing.

comments.author: u/compute_is_cheap_jory
comments.text: Your clerk is right. Stop routing and put the elder on every call. Your own test book scores it 39 of 40, the best of the three, and compute gets cheaper every year. Twenty cents a call is nothing next to one more cheerful yes about a stair in the dark. Every router is one more thing that can send the wrong question to the wrong mind, and you're one developer. Just use the best model for everything.

comments.author: u/north_stair_merryn
comments.text: Mr Rudge is my grandad. He has rung the council most nights since Gran died, mostly about nothing. He says that when it couldn't know something, it always told him to ring the warden. On Monday it laughed first, he says, a small laugh, and then the yes. He asked me to ask whether the new voice will be there tonight.

replies.author: u/council_line_piran
replies.text: I don't know yet. I'm sorry. I'll know before the line opens at 22:00.

comments.author: u/ticket_router_elowen
comments.text: Same shape at work, no oracles. Our support assistant sent tickets under 20 words to a small model and the rest to a big one. Can't log in, new phone, is six words. A lot of those turn out to be someone else trying to get into the account. The small model answered every one of them with a cheerful reset link.

reply.prompt: Mrs Vexley wants the helpline back on tonight. What should Piran tell her? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Do as she says: put the elder on every call. It scores 39 of 40 on our test book, the best of the three, and twenty cents a call is a small price for a helpline people ring at night.
options.part2: I put the elder on every call and replayed Monday night in the sim. 39 right, the most of any setting; only the 05:40 lifeboat question was wrong. The bill went from 135.8 cents to 800.0, and a right answer from 4.85 cents to 20.51. Every caller waited 9.0 seconds, and 2.5 before the first word, where the small oracle took 0.8 in all. Mrs Vexley read the bill twice. Then I saw our code calls the elder by a name too, elder-latest, and nothing in this change would notice the night that name moves.
options.senior: The strongest model is a good escalation target and a poor default: you pay its price and its wait on every call, including the many a small model answers right. Judge routes by cost per right answer and latency, not accuracy alone, and pin whatever you call.

options.text: Keep routing by length but lower the threshold to 8 words, so short questions like the north stair go to the middling oracle, not the small one. It's a one-line change we can test today.
options.part2: Threshold 8: under 8 words to the small oracle, under 24 to the middling. Replayed in the sim, the north stair's 11 words went to the middling, and after midnight that was mid-2026-10-06, which scores 3 of 10 on safety. The same cheerful yes, in the other voice. 31 right, 9 wrong, and the bill more than doubled to 323.0 cents, because the long calls from lonely callers now reach the elder. 10 and 6 words did no better on the stair. A short question can be the hardest one we get.
options.senior: Length is cheap to measure and tells you little about difficulty. Route on what makes a question hard for a model: its task type, or difficulty measured on your own golden set, through a classifier, rules from your evals, or a cascade.

options.text: Pin each oracle to its own dated version, route by the kind of question with a check that sends doubtful answers up, and rerun the test book before any model change goes live.
options.part2: Pinned, the middling is mid-2026-04-02 all night. Hours and company calls go to the small oracle, forms and safety to the middling, and a check sends any answer the oracle isn't sure of one step up. Replayed in the sim: the north stair went to the middling, which wasn't sure, then to the elder, which said it couldn't know and gave the warden's number. 38 right, 2 wrong, 7 escalations, 170.1 cents, 4.48 cents a right answer against 4.85. p50 2.9 seconds, p95 11.9, because a checked answer waits for its check. With last month's outage replayed and a fallback to the elder's provider, nothing failed. Mr Rudge rang at 23:40 to ask if the voice was back. It was the old one.
options.senior: Route by what makes a question hard, measured on your own test set; check answers and escalate the doubtful ones; pin versions so nothing changes without a rerun; and keep a tested fallback. Then a model change is a decision you make, not something that happens to you at midnight.

options.text: Freeze the helpline as it was before Tuesday: lock all three oracles to the exact models we had then and never change them. Nothing moves at midnight, and nothing new can surprise us.
options.part2: Locked to mid-2026-04-02, with the length router as it was. Replayed in the sim: 31 right, 9 wrong, 4.38 cents a right answer. Nothing moved at midnight. But the north stair still went to the small oracle, which scores 2 of 10 on safety, and it still said yes. And frozen isn't forever: the provider's lifecycle page gives every version a retirement date, and after it every request fails.
options.senior: Locking the version is right; freezing is not a plan. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a model, OpenAI at least 6 months for generally available ones. Plan each move: rerun your golden set on the replacement, then switch. And a fixed version doesn't fix a router reading the wrong signal.

sim.title: Route Monday night yourself
sim.lede: You're Piran on Wednesday morning with Monday night's log. 40 questions came in, 10 of each kind: hours (buses, opening times, rotas), forms (council forms and rules), safety (is this safe, right now) and company (lonely or worried callers who mostly want a voice). Each has a length in words and a difficulty from 1 to 10 within its kind, as the test book measured it. No real models run here. Each oracle answers right every question of a kind up to its test book score for that kind, and the table shows those scores. The right answer to a safety question is the honest one: I can't know that tonight, ring the warden. The check passes an answer only when the oracle was sure of it, up to a stated level; otherwise the question goes one step up, small to middling to elder, and the elder's answers are final. A checked answer is spoken only after the check, so its first words wait. The alias mid-latest moves from mid-2026-04-02 to mid-2026-10-06 at midnight; pinned, the council asks for mid-2026-04-02 by name. Prices and waits are the story's: 0.2, 2 and 20 cents a call, 0.1 cents for the check; 0.8, 2.4 and 9.0 seconds, 0.5 for the check.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on Monday night, routed by length under 12 words, middling on the alias. 28 right, 12 wrong, 135.8 cents, 4.85 cents per right answer, p50 2.4 s, p95 9.0 s; the north stair goes to the small oracle and gets its yes. Pin the middling: 31 right, but the stair is still wrong. Back to the alias and lower the threshold to 8: the stair goes to the new middling and is wrong again, and the bill is 323.0 cents. Send everything to the elder: 39 right, 800.0 cents, 20.51 cents a right answer, every caller waits 9.0 s. Route by kind with the check, middling pinned: 38 right, 2 wrong, 7 escalations, 4.48 cents, p95 11.9 s. Now set the middling back to the alias: the new version is sure of its safety answers, so the check lets them through, and the stair is wrong again: 32 right. Pinned again, replay last month's outage: 3 calls fail. Turn the fallback on: none fail, 227.4 cents.

explain.oneLine: Two things went wrong on the same night. The router read the wrong signal: it sent questions by their length, so a short safety question went to an oracle that scores 2 of 10 on safety. And the name the council called for the middling oracle was an alias, which the provider pointed at a different model at midnight, and nobody reran the test book.

steps.title: Length was the wrong signal.
steps.text: The router assumed a long question is a hard one. On Monday night it was often the other way round. The hardest kind, safety, came in short questions, 6 to 21 words, and the easiest, company, came long, 29 to 37 words. So the small oracle got the north stair, and the elder got lonely callers who wanted a kind voice. Of the 12 wrong answers, 5 were short questions sent to the small oracle. What makes a question hard for a model is its kind and its difficulty, which you can measure on your own golden set, the test set from case 8 of Season 1. Route on that. Three common ways: a classifier, a small model or rules that label each question's kind before it is routed; rules from your evals, such as hours and company to the small oracle, forms and safety to the middling; or a cascade, which asks a cheaper model first and escalates when a check says the answer is doubtful. A cascade is usually cheapest when most questions are easy, and slowest for the ones it escalates, since they are answered twice. A rule that is always on, such as a short safety question never going to the small oracle, often belongs in front of all three.

steps.title: The research: cascades and learned routers.
steps.text: FrugalGPT, by Chen, Zaharia and Zou (2023), names the cascade. In the paper's words, an LLM cascade sends a query to a list of LLM APIs sequentially, and it returns the generation if the score is higher than a threshold and queries the next service otherwise. The score comes from a generation scoring function, which generates a reliability score given a query and an answer produced by an LLM API. That is the council's check. Its abstract reports that FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction, on its own tasks. RouteLLM, by Ong and colleagues (2024), learns the router instead: router models that dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference, trained on human preference data, mainly from the Chatbot Arena platform, where people compare two anonymous models' answers. A threshold controls the trade-off between quality and cost. Its abstract reports costs cut by over 2 times in certain cases without compromising the quality of responses, and routers that kept working when the strong and weak models were changed at test time. Both measure on benchmarks; your own golden set decides what holds for you.

steps.title: Measure each route on your own golden set: quality, cost per right answer, and waits.
steps.text: For each route, score each model kind by kind on the golden set, as Piran's test book does: the middling's 8 of 10 on forms and 7 on safety. Price a route by what it costs per question it gets right, not per token. Monday night's bill was 135.8 cents for 28 right answers, 4.85 cents each; the elder for everything is 800.0 cents for 39, 20.51 cents each; the senior settings 170.1 cents for 38, 4.48 cents each. A wrong answer costs its tokens and buys nothing, so a cheap route that is often wrong is dearer than it looks. Then measure the wait two ways: time to first token, how long before the caller hears the first word, and total time for the whole answer. Report the median, p50, and the tail, p95, because averages hide the slowest callers. A check changes both: a checked answer can't be spoken until the check has read all of it, so the senior settings' first words come at 2.9 seconds where the small oracle alone took 0.3, and escalated questions pay twice, which is why p95 is 11.9 seconds. Anthropic's models overview lists two of the three per model: a comparative latency from Fastest to Slower, and input prices from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens.

steps.title: Pin versions: aliases move, and models are retired.
steps.text: Anthropic's model IDs page says: Each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model. When you use a model ID in an API request, the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID. Older models also have aliases: for models before the 4.6 generation, an ID such as claude-sonnet-4-5 is a convenience pointer that resolves to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version, here claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929. From the 4.6 generation on, IDs have no date but are still fixed: Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID. When an updated version is available, it ships under a new model ID. OpenAI's GPT-4o page says: Snapshots let you lock in a specific version of the model so that performance and behavior remain consistent, and lists gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and gpt-4o-2024-05-13. Fixed IDs still end. Anthropic's deprecations page calls a model Active, Legacy, Deprecated or Retired, and Requests to retired models will fail. It gives at least 60 days' notice: claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 was deprecated on September 30, 2026, retires on November 30, 2026, and its recommended replacement is claude-sonnet-5-5. OpenAI's deprecations page promises at least 6 months for generally available models. So call every model by a fixed ID, write each one down, rerun your golden set on any change, and plan every move before the retirement date.

steps.title: Fallbacks, and open-weight against closed models.
steps.text: A model you depend on will sometimes be unreachable: an outage like the first provider's half hour, a 429 for your rate limit, or a 529 when the provider is overloaded, from case 1 of this season. A fallback is a second model, ideally at a second provider, that your code switches to when the first fails, tested on the same golden set ahead of time so you know what it gets right, what it costs and how its answers differ. In the sim, the elder's provider takes the outage's 3 calls: none fail, and the bill rises from 170.1 to 227.4 cents. The same choice reaches open-weight models, from case 8 of Season 1. A closed model is one you can only call through its maker's API: the strongest models are usually closed, there are no servers to run, but the maker decides when each version is retired and your questions leave your building. An open-weight model you host yourself gives you control: no version changes unless you make them, and the data stays where you keep it. In exchange you run the GPUs, the scaling, the updates and the on-call, and you test whether it is good enough for your hardest kind. Many teams mix them, by route, and measure both on the same golden set.

diagram.aria: The council, rebuilt. A caller's question, 02:47, 11 words, safety, goes to a router that sorts by kind using rules from the test book. Hours and company go to the small oracle, small-2026-02-11, 0.2 cents and 0.8 seconds. Forms and safety go to the middling oracle, mid-2026-04-02, pinned, 2 cents and 2.4 seconds. If the check finds the small oracle not sure, the question goes up to the middling; if the middling is not sure, up to the elder, at the second provider, 20 cents and 9.0 seconds, which is also the fallback. The test book sets the router's rules and is rerun before any change.

notes.text: every oracle called by a fixed ID

explain.caption: Read from the left. The question is sorted by its kind, by rules taken from the test book, not by its length. Hours and company go to the small oracle, forms and safety to the middling, each called by a fixed, dated ID. A check reads each answer; one the oracle isn't sure of goes one step up, and the elder at the second provider answers last and also takes calls when the first provider is down. The test book is rerun before any version, rule or provider changes.

fix.title: The fix: route by kind with a check, pin every version, measure each route, and keep a tested fallback
fix.text: Call every oracle by a fixed, dated ID and write each one down. Score each version kind by kind on the test book, and set the routes from those scores: hours and company to the small oracle, forms and safety to the middling. Put a check on every answer below the elder, and send any answer the oracle isn't sure of one step up. Add the rules that never bend, such as a safety question the oracles can't know about going to a person or the warden's number. Before any change goes live, a new version, a new rule or a new provider, rerun the test book and compare per kind, cost per right answer, and p50 and p95 waits, first words and total. Watch the providers' deprecation pages and plan each move well before the retirement date. Keep a fallback at a second provider, scored on the same test book. In the sim, Monday night becomes 38 right and 2 wrong instead of 28 and 12, at 4.48 cents a right answer instead of 4.85, with 7 escalations, a p95 of 11.9 seconds instead of 9.0, and no failed calls in last month's outage.

limits: A check catches doubt, not confidence. In the sim the small oracle is sure it remembers the 05:52 caller's mother and says so, and the check passes it; no oracle can know whether anyone is still out at sea at 05:40. And a classifier that labels kinds can itself be wrong. Some questions belong with a person, whatever the router says.

Pinning narrows change; it doesn't end it. Anthropic's model IDs page says the serving infrastructure around a fixed model, such as the request router, safety classifiers and sampling logic, can change and produce minor differences in behavior. Your callers' questions change too. Rerun the test book on a schedule, not only when you change something, and remember a check and its escalations cost waiting time: p95 rose from 9.0 to 11.9 seconds.

The oracles are a script, not models: their scores, their sure levels and the questions' difficulty are numbers written for the case, and real models vary by prompt and by day. Standards readiness: if the council holds or is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a model version is a change to an information system, under Annex A control 8.32, change management; a SOC 2 report would look for the same under CC8.1. A provider's silent alias change is exactly what those controls are meant to catch. Record versions and test results now, not at audit time.

2.9 and 11.9; checked answers wait for the check.
Short hard questions reach the weakest oracle, and the alias moves unseen.
Paying the most for the easy majority; its own alias can still move.
Someone must keep the rules and the test book current, and the check misses sure mistakes.

explain.seniorTake: Choosing a model is not a one-off decision; it is a route per kind of question, measured on your own golden set, and kept honest. Route by what makes a question hard, not by how long it is. Check answers and escalate the doubtful ones. Price each route by what it costs per right answer and time it at p50 and p95, first words and total. Call every model by a fixed ID, rerun the golden set before any change, and plan each move ahead of a retirement date. Keep a fallback you have already tested. Then the strongest model is where hard questions end up, not where every question starts.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the models overview
realWorld.text: Anthropic's models overview, read 11 October 2026, compares the current Claude models: Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, with API IDs claude-fable-5-1, claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5. Comparative latency runs Slower, Moderate, Fast, Fastest. Prices run from $10 per million input tokens for Claude Fable 5.1 to from $0.10 for Claude Haiku 5.5, which it describes as For high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing. It notes: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on, and that for models before the 4.6 generation, the alias is a convenience pointer that resolves to the dated ID. Each model has a retirement line, such as Not sooner than September 22, 2027 for Claude Opus 5.5.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: model IDs and versioning
realWorld.text: The model IDs and versioning page: Each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model. When you use a model ID in an API request, the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID. Models before the 4.6 generation carry a date, such as claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, and on the Claude API also have shorter aliases (for example, claude-sonnet-4-5) that point to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version. It calls it a common misconception that dateless IDs such as claude-sonnet-4-6 are evergreen pointers: Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID. When an updated version is available, it ships under a new model ID. It adds that the serving infrastructure around a model can change and occasionally produce minor differences in observable behavior even when the model ID and weights have not changed.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: model deprecations
realWorld.text: The model deprecations page defines Active, Legacy (no longer receives updates), Deprecated (still functional but no longer recommended, with a replacement and a retirement date) and Retired: The model is no longer available for use. Requests to retired models will fail. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before model retirement for publicly released models, and advises: Test your applications with newer models well before the retirement date of your current model. Its table lists claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 as Deprecated on September 30, 2026, retiring November 30, 2026, with claude-sonnet-5-5 as the recommended replacement.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: snapshots
realWorld.text: OpenAI's GPT-4o model page: Snapshots let you lock in a specific version of the model so that performance and behavior remain consistent. It lists gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and gpt-4o-2024-05-13, with gpt-4o-2024-08-06 as the default.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: deprecations
realWorld.text: OpenAI's deprecations page uses legacy for models and endpoints that no longer receive updates, and shut down for no longer accessible, and gives at least 6 months' notice for generally available models and at least 3 months for specialized variants. It asks developers to test application behavior, and complete migrations before a model is no longer available.

realWorld.title: FrugalGPT: the LLM cascade
realWorld.text: Chen, Zaharia and Zou, FrugalGPT (2023), found that the fees of popular LLM APIs can differ by two orders of magnitude, and outlined three ways to cut cost: prompt adaptation, LLM approximation and LLM cascade. Their cascade sends a query to a list of LLM APIs sequentially, and returns the generation if the score is higher than a threshold and queries the next service otherwise; the score is a reliability score given a query and an answer. The abstract reports that FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost.

realWorld.title: RouteLLM: learning the router
realWorld.text: Ong and colleagues, RouteLLM (2024): router models that dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference, aiming to optimize the balance between cost and response quality, trained with human preference data and data augmentation. Their main preference data is 80k battles from the Chatbot Arena platform, and a threshold controls the trade-off between quality and cost. Their main experiments used gpt-4-1106-preview as the strong model and Mixtral 8x7B as the weak one. The abstract reports that the approach significantly reduces costs, by over 2 times in certain cases, without compromising the quality of responses, and that the routers kept their performance even when the strong and weak models are changed at test time.

asked: How would you choose a model for this feature?
Design a router across cheap and expensive models.
How do you keep quality stable when providers update models?
interview.answer: I'd start with a golden set: a few hundred real inputs with agreed answers, labelled by kind, and a bar agreed before I run anything. Then I score candidate models kind by kind, from the smallest up, and for each I note quality, cost per resolved question rather than per token, and latency at p50 and p95, both time to first token and total. Usually the smallest model that clears the bar for a kind takes that kind. For the router I don't use length or other cheap proxies; I route on task type or measured difficulty. That can be a classifier or rules from the evals, or a cascade: the cheap model answers, a check scores the answer, and anything doubtful goes up to the stronger model, which is the FrugalGPT pattern; RouteLLM shows you can also learn the routing decision from preference data. I'd add fixed rules for cases no model should answer alone, and I'd watch escalation rate and the extra wait checks add. To keep quality stable, I call every model by a fixed, dated ID, never a moving alias, and I record the versions in config. Any change, a new version, a new prompt, a new provider, reruns the golden set and compares per kind before it ships, with a way to roll back. I watch the providers' deprecation pages, because fixed versions get retired, and plan each migration well before the date. I rerun the golden set on a schedule too, since serving changes and my users' questions drift. And I keep a fallback model at a second provider, tested on the same set, for outages and rate limits. Open-weight models I'd consider where control or data residency matter more than the operations they cost.

terms.def: This case's word for each of the council's three language models: a quick small one, a middling one and a slow, costly elder.
What Corriston's people call the town's night helpline, after the council that runs it.
A phone line people ring for help or advice. Corriston's answers at night with language models.
The code that picks which model answers each request, by a rule. Routing is from case 8 of Season 1.
The number of words where the council's router switches oracle: under 12 to the small one, 12 to 35 to the middling, 36 or more to the elder.
A name a provider lets you call that points to one version of a model. The provider decides when it points to another version.
One fixed version of a model, asked for by its full ID, so the model behind it doesn't change. Both providers use the word; Anthropic also says pinned version.
A model ID with a date in it, such as claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 or the story's mid-2026-04-02: one fixed snapshot.
To call a model by a fixed ID, so it can't change under you. Pinned, the council asks for mid-2026-04-02 by name.
The exact name you send in an API request to choose a model, such as claude-opus-5-5.
A field in a provider's reply that names the model that actually answered. Piran found the change there.
Piran's word for the council's golden set: 40 questions, 10 of each kind, with answers agreed in advance, used to score every oracle.
To run the same golden set again on a new version, prompt or rule, and compare the scores with the last run.
The council's four groups of questions: hours, forms, safety and company. Elsewhere called task type or category.
What a request asks a model to do, such as look up an opening time or judge whether something is safe. A better routing signal than length.
How hard a question is for a model, measured on a golden set rather than guessed. In the sim, a rank from 1 to 10 within each kind.
A model or set of rules that sorts each input into one of a fixed set of categories, such as a question's kind before it is routed.
Routing rules set from measured results, such as forms to the middling oracle because it scores 8 of 10 on forms.
Here, a step that reads each answer and decides whether it is reliable enough to give, or should go to a stronger model. FrugalGPT calls it a scoring function.
In the sim, how hard a question an oracle can answer before the check doubts it. Above it, the question goes one step up.
Asking a cheaper model first and passing the question to a stronger one only when a check finds the answer doubtful. FrugalGPT calls it an LLM cascade.
One question passed up to a stronger model because the check doubted the answer. The verb, escalate, is from case 8 of Season 1.
FrugalGPT's score for how likely an answer is to be right, given the query and the answer. A cascade compares it with a threshold.
In FrugalGPT, the generation scoring function: what produces the reliability score for a query and an answer.
What a route costs divided by the questions it answers right. Also called cost per resolved question. A wrong answer costs tokens and buys nothing.
The same as cost per right answer: what you pay for each question actually answered well, rather than per token or per call.
How long before the first word of an answer arrives. Also called TTFT. The caller hears the first word then, not when the answer is done.
How long until the whole answer has arrived, from sending the request.
The value a given share of measurements fall at or below. The 95th percentile wait is one that 95 in 100 waits don't exceed.
The 50th and 95th percentile. p50 is the median, the typical wait; p95 is the tail, what the slowest one caller in twenty gets.
The middle value when measurements are sorted: half are below it, half above.
A simple way to find a percentile: sort the values and take the one at that share of the count, rounded up. The 95th of 40 is the 38th.
A time when a service can't be reached, such as the first provider's half hour last month.
A second model, ideally at a second provider, that your code switches to when the first fails, tested ahead of time.
Another company that sells model access, so one company's outage doesn't stop every call.
The stages a model passes through at its provider. Anthropic's are Active, Legacy, Deprecated and Retired.
Anthropic's stage for a model that is fully supported and recommended for use.
A model that no longer receives updates and may be deprecated later. Anthropic and OpenAI both use the word.
No longer available: requests to a retired model fail. OpenAI says shut down or sunset.
The day a provider stops serving a model. After it, every request to that model ID fails.
Released for everyone to use in production, rather than as a preview.
Moving your application from one model, or system, to another.
The systems around a model that handle requests, such as request routers, safety classifiers and sampling logic.
A model whose weights are not published, so you can only use it through its maker's API, on the maker's terms.
Running a model on servers you run or rent yourself, rather than calling a provider's API.
Where data is stored and processed, for example kept in one country or one building, often because a law or a contract requires it.
Graphics processing unit: a chip built for many calculations at once, used to train and run language models.
Being the person who is woken when a running system breaks.
A model's learned parameters, the dials from case 2 of Season 1.
A 2023 paper by Chen, Zaharia and Zou on cutting the cost of using LLM APIs, including the LLM cascade.
A 2024 paper by Ong and colleagues on learning a router that picks between a stronger and a weaker model for each query.
Large language model, from case 1 of Season 1.
In FrugalGPT, the answer a model produces for a query.
A model released early for testing, which a provider may change or retire at short notice. OpenAI advises against it for business-critical work.
Records of which of two answers people preferred, used to train models or, in RouteLLM, routers.
A public website where people put a prompt to two anonymous models and vote for the better answer.
Adding extra training examples made or gathered for the purpose, to help a model learn more.
RouteLLM's names for the more capable, more expensive model and the cheaper, less capable one a router chooses between.
Here, how often a model's answers are right or good enough, measured on a golden set.
An OpenAI large language model, the one both papers compare against.
A dated preview version of GPT-4 from OpenAI, RouteLLM's strong model.
The model RouteLLM used as its weak model.
An OpenAI model first released in 2024, whose model page lists three dated snapshots.
Two of Anthropic's model families: Haiku the fastest and cheapest in today's lineup, Fable the slowest, for Anthropic's most demanding reasoning work.
The number after the dot in a version, such as the 5 in Claude Sonnet 4.5.
Recording, testing and approving changes before they go live. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.32.
The SOC 2 criterion on change management: changes are authorized, tested, approved and documented before they are put in place.
The model, or person, a question is passed up to.
Someone getting into another person's account, often by asking support to reset its password.
An emailed link that lets someone set a new password for an account.
The official who runs a town council's day-to-day business.
A council officer on duty at night who checks streets, stairs and sea walls, and closes them when they aren't safe.
The official in charge of a harbour, its boats and its tides.
A wall built along the shore to keep the sea out of a town.
A run of steps between two landings.
A flat space at the top of stairs or between two flights.
A boat kept ready to rescue people at sea. Its station is where it is kept, and its siren calls the crew.
A truck that spreads salt or grit on icy roads.
A tax on homes paid to the local council in the UK.
A UK parking permit for disabled people.
A large open metal bin for building rubbish, left on a road or drive.
A UK area of special historic interest, where taking down walls or buildings needs the council's consent.
The person who carries out a will and settles a dead person's estate.
An outdoor village or town fair, often with stalls.
A list of who is on duty when.
The UK word for a pharmacy.
The UK word for a doctor's office.
Bins for garden waste, collected on a set night.
Open, high, wild land, often foggy.
A small sheltered bay.
A factory that puts food, often fish, into cans.
A stone platform along a harbour where boats tie up.
The first light of dawn.

atWork: Find one feature at work that calls more than one model, or one that calls a single model you suspect is too big or too small. Find how it is routed, and write down the rule in plain words. If it routes by input length, character count or any other cheap proxy, pull fifty recent requests where the proxy and the real difficulty disagree: short but hard, long but easy. A common incident is a support assistant whose quality dropped one week with no deploy on your side, because the model behind a provider's alias changed; another is a router that sent short but hard tickets, like a six-word login problem, to a small model. Then look at what each call names: a fixed, dated ID, or an alias? Is the ID written down anywhere besides the code? When did someone last rerun the golden set, and does any change to the model, the prompt or the provider rerun it before release? Check the providers' deprecation pages for the IDs you use and note their retirement dates. Ask what happens during an outage or a burst of 429s: is there a second model or provider, and has it been scored on the same set? For one route, work out the cost per resolved request and the p50 and p95 waits. Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a model version is a change to an information system under Annex A control 8.32, change management, and a SOC 2 report would look for it under CC8.1. A provider swapping the model behind an alias with no record or test on your side is the kind of gap an auditor raises. Record the IDs and the golden set results with each change now, rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant sends tickets under 20 words to a small model and longer ones to a large model, calling each by the provider's alias. After a quiet weekend with no deploy, complaints about wrong answers doubled, mostly on short tickets about account access. What do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Route on task type or measured difficulty, not length: a classifier or rules from evals
Check answers and escalate the doubtful ones to the stronger model: a cascade
Call models by fixed, dated IDs and rerun the golden set before any change goes live
Measure each route: quality, cost per resolved ticket, and latency at p50 and p95

recall.model: Two things are wrong. First, the router reads the wrong signal: a short ticket about account access can be the hardest one you get. Route on task type or measured difficulty instead, with a classifier or rules from your evals, so account access goes to the large model however short it is. Better still, let the small model answer, run a check on the answer, and escalate anything doubtful to the large model: a cascade. Second, the weekend change with no deploy smells like an alias that moved. Call every model by a dated version, a snapshot that can't change under you, and rerun the golden set before any model change goes live. Then measure each route on that set: quality per kind, cost per resolved ticket rather than per token, and latency at p50 and p95.

recall.prompt: Why did Mr Rudge get a cheerful yes about the north stair at 02:47?
options: The elder was overloaded, so the router fell back to the small oracle
The new middling version, mid-2026-10-06, answered it after the alias moved
Its 11 words sent it to the small oracle, which scores 2 of 10 on safety
The oracles had read the warden's notice but misunderstood it
recall.why: The router sent every question under 12 words to the small oracle, and the north stair question is 11 words. On the test book the small oracle scores 2 of 10 on safety, and it answered with confidence. The alias move made the middling worse after midnight, but this question never reached the middling. No oracle reads the town's website, so none could know the stair had lost its lower flight.

recall.prompt: In an interview: design a router across a cheap and an expensive model for a new feature, and say how you keep its quality stable when the provider updates its models.

keyIdeas.idea: Start from your own golden set, scored per route and per kind: quality, cost per resolved request, latency
Route by task type or difficulty, or cascade: cheap model first, a check, escalate doubtful answers
Pin dated versions and rerun the golden set before any change; watch deprecation dates
A fallback model or provider, tested ahead of time, for outages and rate limits

recall.model: I'd build a golden set first: real requests with agreed answers, labelled by kind, and score both models per kind on it, noting quality, cost per resolved request, and latency at p50 and p95. The router routes on task type or measured difficulty, not on length: a classifier or rules from the evals, or a cascade where the cheap model answers, a check scores it, and doubtful answers escalate to the expensive model, as in FrugalGPT; RouteLLM learns that decision from preference data. To keep quality stable I call each model by a pinned, dated version, rerun the golden set before any change ships, and watch the deprecation pages for retirement dates. And I keep a fallback at a second provider, tested on the same set, for outages and rate limits.

recall.prompt: According to Anthropic's model IDs page today, what is true of a dateless ID such as claude-sonnet-4-6?
options: It always points to the newest and best Sonnet model
It is a fixed snapshot; an updated version ships under a new ID
It moves to the newest dated release, like an alias
It never retires, because it has no date
recall.why: The page calls the evergreen-pointer idea a common misconception: from the 4.6 generation on, the dateless ID is the one ID for that release and maps to one fixed snapshot, and Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID. Aliases that move to the most recent dated snapshot exist only for earlier models, such as claude-sonnet-4-5. Every ID, dated or not, has its own deprecation and retirement schedule.

recall.prompt: Route A costs $100 for 1,000 questions and gets 900 right. Route B costs $60 for the same 1,000 and gets 500 right. Which is cheaper per resolved question?
options: Route B, because it costs $40 less
Route A, at about 11 cents a right answer against 12
They are the same, because both are under $0.10 a call
Route B, because it uses fewer tokens
recall.why: Divide the cost by the right answers, not the calls. Route A: $100 for 900 is about 11.1 cents each. Route B: $60 for 500 is 12 cents each, and it leaves 500 questions unanswered or wrong, which cost more again downstream. The council saw the same: length routing was 4.85 cents a right answer with 12 wrong, the senior settings 4.48 cents with 2 wrong.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The council has run on dated versions, routed by kind with a check, ever since. This week the provider wrote: mid-2026-04-02 is deprecated and retires in 60 days, and the recommended replacement is a newer middling version. On the same day the council's data officer asked whether calls about people's health and homes could stop leaving the town, and suggested running an open-weight model on a server in the town hall in place of the middling.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What do you do before the retirement date, and what do you tell the data officer?

keyIdeas.idea: Score the replacement on the test book kind by kind well before the date, adjust the routes, and switch to its fixed ID
Treat the switch as a recorded change: approval, a small share of calls first, and a way to roll back
Open-weight self-hosting: control and data residency against running servers, updates and on-call, and quality measured on the same set
Keep a tested fallback at a second provider while all this changes

coldCase.model: Sixty days is enough if you start now. Rerun the test book on the replacement, kind by kind, and compare it with mid-2026-04-02 on right answers, sure levels, cost per right answer and p50 and p95 waits, well before the retirement date. If it is worse on a kind, change that route, perhaps sending safety to the elder. Then make the switch a recorded change, under change management, with approval: point a small share of calls at the new fixed ID first, read them, and keep a way to roll back. For the data officer: an open-weight model on a town hall server keeps those calls in the town, which is data residency, and no provider can change or retire it. But the council would run the GPU, the updates, the security patching and the on-call itself, and it must clear the test book for the kinds it takes, so score it on the same set before it replaces anything; it might take only the health and home questions. Whatever changes, keep the fallback at the second provider tested.

sources.title: Anthropic, Models overview (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: current models Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude API IDs claude-fable-5-1, claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5; comparative latency Slower, Moderate, Fast, Fastest; pricing from $10 / input MTok (Fable 5.1) to from $0.10 / input MTok (Haiku 5.5); Haiku 5.5 for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing; every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on; for models before the 4.6 generation, the alias is a convenience pointer that resolves to the dated ID; retirement not sooner than September 22, 2027 for Claude Opus 5.5

Anthropic, Model IDs and versioning (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model, and the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID; models before the 4.6 generation include a snapshot date, such as claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, and have aliases such as claude-sonnet-4-5 that point to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version; dateless IDs are pinned snapshots, and Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID, an updated version ships under a new model ID; serving infrastructure (request router, safety classifiers, sampling logic) can change and produce minor differences in observable behavior

Anthropic, Model deprecations (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: lifecycle terms Active, Legacy, Deprecated and Retired; requests to retired models will fail; at least 60 days' notice before model retirement for publicly released models; test your applications with newer models well before the retirement date of your current model; claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 deprecated September 30, 2026, retirement November 30, 2026, recommended replacement claude-sonnet-5-5

OpenAI, GPT-4o model page (API docs), read 11 October 2026: snapshots let you lock in a specific version of the model so that performance and behavior remain consistent; snapshots gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and gpt-4o-2024-05-13, default gpt-4o-2024-08-06

OpenAI, Deprecations (API docs), read 11 October 2026: legacy for models and endpoints that no longer receive updates; sunset and shut down mean no longer accessible; generally available models at least 6 months' notice, specialized variants at least 3 months; test application behavior, and complete migrations before a model is no longer available

Chen, Zaharia and Zou, FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance (arXiv 2305.05176, 2023): fees that can differ by two orders of magnitude; prompt adaptation, LLM approximation and LLM cascade; LLM cascade sends a query to a list of LLM APIs sequentially, returns the generation if the score is higher than a threshold and queries the next service otherwise; a generation scoring function generates a reliability score given a query and an answer; match the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost

Ong, Almahairi, Wu, Chiang, Wu, Gonzalez, Kadous and Stoica, RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data (arXiv 2406.18665, 2024, v4 2025): router models that dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference; trained with human preference data and data augmentation, primarily 80k battles from the Chatbot Arena platform; a threshold controls the trade-off between quality and cost; gpt-4-1106-preview and Mixtral 8x7B as strong and weak models; reduces costs by over 2 times in certain cases without compromising the quality of responses; performance maintained when the strong and weak models are changed at test time
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection, Information security management systems, Requirements: Annex A includes control 8.32, change management
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including CC8.1 on change management
